clinicalPearls: Respiratory diphtheria is clinically diagnosed by the constellation of sore throat, adherent tonsillar/pharyngeal/nasal pseudomembranous lesions, and low-grade fever (p.1223).

The diphtheritic pseudomembrane is gray or whitish and sharply demarcated; unlike the exudate of streptococcal pharyngitis it is tightly adherent to underlying tissue, and attempts to dislodge it may cause bleeding (p.1223).
A few patients develop 'bull-neck' diphtheria from edema of the submandibular and paratracheal region, with massive tonsillar swelling, foul breath, thick speech, and stridorous breathing (p.1223).

Diphtheria should be considered in any patient with severe pharyngitis, especially with difficulty swallowing, respiratory compromise, or signs of systemic disease (myocarditis, generalized weakness); a pharyngeal pseudomembrane or extensive exudate should prompt consideration (p.1222-1223).

Toxigenic strains most often cause pharyngeal disease, while nontoxigenic strains commonly cause cutaneous disease; in tropical latitudes cutaneous diphtheria is more common than respiratory diphtheria (p.1221-1222).
Once a clinical diagnosis is made, diphtheria antitoxin should be obtained and administered as rapidly as possible because antitoxin cannot neutralize cell-bound toxin (p.1224).
Hoarseness suggests laryngeal diphtheria, in which laryngoscopy may be diagnostically helpful (p.1223).
Antibiotics in diphtheria are used primarily to prevent transmission to contacts and to halt further toxin production; they are not a substitute for antitoxin (p.1224).

Patients who recover should be vaccinated, since natural infection does not reliably confer protective immunity; antitoxin levels should be measured (6 months after antitoxin administration) (p.1224).
harrison.pathophysiology: Disease is driven by diphtheria toxin produced by toxigenic (tox+) strains of C. diphtheriae. The tox structural gene is carried by lysogenic corynebacteriophage beta, and nontoxigenic strains can be converted to the toxigenic phenotype; iron-limiting conditions optimize toxin expression. The toxin is a single-chain 535-amino-acid protein produced in the pharyngeal pseudomembranous lesion, taken up into the bloodstream and distributed to all organs. After binding its receptor (a heparin-binding EGF-like precursor) it is internalized by receptor-mediated endocytosis; the A fragment enters the cytosol and irreversibly inhibits protein synthesis via NAD+-dependent ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2, causing cell death. Pseudomembranes consist of an inner fibrin band and a luminal neutrophil band overlying toxin-induced mucosal ulcers with edema, hyperemia, and vascular congestion; initially white and firmly adherent, they turn gray/green/black as necrosis advances and may extend into bronchial airways (p.1221-1223).
infectionMimics: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis (exudative, but its exudate is not tightly adherent unlike the diphtheritic pseudomembrane) (p.1223)
Respiratory virus pharyngitis (rhinovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, coronavirus, adenovirus) (p.1223)
Herpes simplex virus and Epstein-Barr virus (infectious mononucleosis) pharyngitis (p.1223)
Atypical bacterial pharyngitis (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae) (p.1223)
Acute HIV infection, gonococcal pharyngitis, and fusobacterial infection / Lemierre's syndrome (p.1223)
Corynebacterium ulcerans / C. pseudotuberculosis, which express the same toxin and cause diphtheria-like disease (p.1222)
additionalInvestigations: Culture of pseudomembrane fragments or submembranous swabs on selective medium (Loffler's or Tinsdale's, tellurite/colistin/nalidixic-acid based) plus nonselective medium such as blood agar (p.1223-1224)
Histopathologic demonstration of compatible gram-positive organisms / characteristic local lesions (p.1223-1224)
Notify the laboratory that diphtheria is being considered so special selective medium and biochemical differentiation from commensal corynebacteria are performed (p.1224)
Toxigenicity testing; report all toxigenic C. diphtheriae isolates to the state health department (reportable disease) (p.1224)
Nasopharyngeal culture in patients with cutaneous diphtheria (p.1224)
Repeat throat culture ~2 weeks after completing antimicrobial therapy to document eradication (p.1224)
Cardiac workup to assess for myocarditis (p.1225)
Antitoxin (antibody) titer measurement after recovery, performed 6 months after antitoxin administration (p.1224)
redFlags: Neck (submandibular/paratracheal) edema and difficulty breathing in advanced cases carry a poor prognosis (p.1223)

Airway obstruction is a major early risk and accounts for 60-65% of deaths, usually in the first 1-2 weeks; sloughing pseudomembranes may obstruct the airway or extend to larynx/tracheobronchial tree (children especially prone) (p.1224)
Toxic cardiomyopathy/myocarditis (cardiac arrhythmias or congestive heart failure), a late manifestation arising >=1 week after respiratory symptoms, accounting for 20-25% of deaths (p.1223-1224)
Bull-neck diphtheria, ventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, or complete heart block (p.1224)

Polyneuropathy 3-5 weeks after onset: cranial nerve involvement (lingual/facial numbness, dysphonia, dysphagia), then weakness of respiratory and abdominal muscles, limb paresis, sensory ataxia, and autonomic dysfunction with hypotension (~15% of deaths) (p.1224)
Large or extensive pseudomembranes and laryngeal/tracheal/bronchial involvement indicate severe disease and poor prognosis (p.1223-1224)
harrison.prognosis: A systematic review of >20 outbreaks found a case-fatality ratio of 29% among unvaccinated, untreated individuals, with children under 5 at 1.5-fold higher mortality risk. Fatal pseudomembranous diphtheria typically occurs in unimmunized patients or those with nonprotective antibody titers. Risk factors for death include bull-neck diphtheria; myocarditis with ventricular tachycardia; atrial fibrillation; complete heart block; age >60 or <6 months; alcoholism; extensive pseudomembrane elongation; and laryngeal/tracheal/bronchial involvement. A key predictor of fatal outcome is the interval between onset of local disease and administration of antitoxin. Cutaneous diphtheria has a low mortality rate and is rarely associated with myocarditis or peripheral neuropathy. Polyneuropathy is typically reversible in patients who survive the acute phase (p.1224-1225).
pitfalls: Antitoxin cannot neutralize cell-bound toxin, so delay in administration worsens outcome; do not wait for laboratory confirmation once diphtheria is clinically suspected (p.1224).
Antibiotics are not a substitute for antitoxin; they mainly prevent transmission and further toxin production (p.1224).
Glucocorticoids have NOT been shown to reduce the risk of myocarditis or polyneuropathy (p.1225).

Cutaneous diphtheria lesions are not characteristic and are indistinguishable from other dermatoses, so diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation; the punched-out appearance is only occasional, not consistent (p.1224).
Corynebacterium pseudodiphtheriticum is a nontoxigenic normal throat commensal and does not pose significant risk; it must be differentiated from C. diphtheriae (p.1224).
Drug-resistant and multidrug-resistant C. diphtheriae strains exist and are increasing; consider resistance when eradication efforts fail (p.1224).
Natural infection does not reliably confer immunity, so survivors must be vaccinated (p.1224).
harrison.severityClassification: CDC case definitions: confirmed respiratory diphtheria (laboratory proven or epidemiologically linked to a culture-confirmed case) vs probable respiratory diphtheria (clinically compatible but not laboratory proven or epidemiologically linked). Carriers are individuals with positive C. diphtheriae cultures who are asymptomatic or symptomatic but lack pseudomembranes (p.1223).
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e, Ch.155 (Diphtheria and Other Corynebacterial Infections), pp.1221-1225
Sharma NC et al: Diphtheria. Nat Rev Dis Primers 5:81, 2019
management: Diphtheria antitoxin administered urgently on clinical suspicion, before laboratory confirmation, since it neutralises only circulating and not cell-bound toxin
Antimicrobial eradication of the organism with a macrolide such as erythromycin or azithromycin, or penicillin, to halt toxin production and transmission
Airway management with close monitoring for obstruction and bull-neck disease, involving ENT and anaesthetics, with intubation or tracheostomy as required
Cardiac monitoring for toxin-mediated myocarditis with treatment of arrhythmia and heart failure, and neurological monitoring for palatal and other palsies
Strict droplet isolation with supportive care and bed rest
Documented eradication by repeat cultures after therapy, with treatment of carriers
Contact tracing, chemoprophylaxis and vaccination of contacts, active immunisation of the patient during convalescence, and statutory notification to public health
